findings.summary: The "Signals 101" page teaches trap invocation, reset, ignore and the one-slot rule — the whole subject of page 2 — and page 2 then re-teaches the same three forms.
findings.evidence: Page 1 ends with ["trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM HUP  # 4-net","trap - INT      # restore default","trap '' INT     # ignore; kids inherit","trap -p EXIT    # print just this one"] plus the callout "One Slot Per Signal: A second `trap ... INT` silently replaces the first." Page 2's "Disarm vs Ignore" table repeats them: ["`trap - INT`","default action","default"], ["`trap '' INT`","ignored","inherit ignore"].
findings.fix: Cut the second code block and the "One Slot Per Signal" callout from page 1 and let page 2's "The Form" / "Disarm vs Ignore" sections be their first appearance; keep page 1 to signal identity, numbering, exit-status arithmetic and real-vs-pseudo.

findings.summary: `set -e` (and on page 2 `set -E`/`set -T`) carry load-bearing claims about when traps fire, but neither is defined until page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "Normal end of script, explicit `exit`, `set -e` abort" and "`set -e` mid-cleanup can skip the rest of teardown". Page 2: "ERR/DEBUG/RETURN skip subshells unless `set -E`/`set -T`". The definitions appear only on page 7: "`set -euo pipefail`: exit on error, unset var, pipe failure" and the errtrace callout "`set -E` fixes exactly that".
findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss at first use — on page 2, "`set -E` = errtrace, makes ERR inherit; `set -T` does the same for DEBUG/RETURN (page 7)"; on page 3, "`set -e` = abort the script on any uncaught non-zero command" — or move the strict-mode section ahead of the EXIT chapter.

findings.summary: The page 4/5 boundary is offset from the topic boundary in both directions: page 4 closes by introducing background jobs and `$!`, and page 5 opens with the leftover temp-file bullets.
findings.evidence: Page 4 ("Temp Files: mktemp, Guards, and Unlink") ends with heading "Capture The PID Now" and "`cmd &` backgrounds; `$!` holds that PID" … "`kill $(jobs -p)` is a quick, non-recursive sweep". Page 5 ("Killing Children: Jobs, PIDs, Groups") opens with an unheaded bullets block: "On failure keep the dir: `[[ $rc -eq 0 ]] || echo \"kept: $tmpdir\"`", "`mkfifo` pipes need the same trap treatment", "Lock files: `flock` an fd that closes on exit".
findings.fix: Swap the two blocks: move "Capture The PID Now" to the top of page 5 as its opening section, and move the keep-on-failure / mkfifo / flock bullets to page 4 under a heading such as "Other Resources, Same Trap".

findings.summary: The `set -m` callout is backwards: enabling job control puts every background job in its own process group, so `kill -- -$$` stops reaching the children it is supposed to sweep.
findings.evidence: "`set -m` turns on job control so your script leads its own group. Without it, `kill -- -$$` can hit the caller's interactive shell." plus the table row "whole group | `kill -- -$$` | entire tree"
findings.fix: Replace with: a script launched from an interactive shell is already a process-group leader ($$ == PGID), so `kill -- -$$` targets its own group; `set -m` instead gives each background job its own group, which is what makes `kill -- -$!` work per job. Also soften "entire tree" to "everyone still in this process group" — children that call setsid or start their own group escape.

findings.summary: The strict-mode code sample claims `false | true` prints PIPESTATUS[0] as 1, but under `set -Eeuo pipefail` errexit kills the script at that pipeline so the `echo` never runs.
findings.fix: Either drop `-e`/`pipefail` from the sample (`set -o pipefail` alone) or write `false | true || true; echo "${PIPESTATUS[0]}"  # 1`, and state explicitly that with `pipefail` + `-e` the pipeline itself aborts the script after firing ERR.

findings.summary: The comment on the re-raise code line is clipped at the right edge of its code block, cutting the exit status value.
findings.evidence: Code block reads `trap - INT; kill -INT "$$"   # true 13` with the final character of "130" sliced by the block's right border.
findings.fix: Shorten the inline comment (e.g. `# true 130` → `# 130`) or let the code block wrap/shrink the font so the full line fits inside its frame.

findings.summary: The Ctrl-C page ends with an unlabelled strict-mode/ERR code block that uses `set -Eeuo pipefail`, `$BASH_COMMAND` and `PIPESTATUS` before page 7 defines any of them, and page 7 is then left without its own ERR-handler example.
findings.evidence: Page 6 final block: ["set -Eeuo pipefail","trap 'echo \"L$LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND\"' ERR","false | true; echo \"${PIPESTATUS[0]}\"  # 1"] — page 7 only later says "`set -euo pipefail`: exit on error, unset var, pipe failure" and lists "`$BASH_COMMAND` | the failing command" in its "Stack Trace Fields" table. The `# 1` result silently depends on pipefail semantics that are never stated on page 6.
findings.fix: Move this code block to page 7, placing it directly after the "Strict Mode Triple" section (and before/adjacent to "Stack Trace Fields"), so it becomes the ERR chapter's worked example; end page 6 with the double-Ctrl-C sidebox instead.

findings.summary: The double-Ctrl-C pattern is asserted but the only example shows the counter running in the main script flow, outside any trap, so the mechanism it claims is never demonstrated.
findings.evidence: Sidebox says "Count handler invocations in a variable / First: graceful cleanup and message / Second: skip cleanup, hard-kill the group", but the accompanying code is ["sleep 30 & wait $!   # trap fires promptly","hits=$((hits+1))","(( hits > 1 )) && kill -9 -$$   # 2nd Ctrl-C"] — `hits` is never initialised and never incremented inside a handler, and line 1 belongs to a different pattern.
findings.fix: Split into two blocks: keep "sleep 30 & wait $!" with the wait-latency table, and show the counter inside a handler, e.g. `hits=0; on_int(){ hits=$((hits+1)); (( hits > 1 )) && kill -9 -$$; cleanup; trap - INT; kill -INT "$$"; }; trap on_int INT`.

findings.summary: `$$` is used in a page-1 sidebox and code with no definition, and is never defined anywhere in the part.
findings.evidence: Page 1 sidebox "Same Signal, Two Origins": "`kill -INT $$`: goes to your shell only", and code "kill -INT \"$$\"        # scripted, not typed". It recurs on pages 5 and 6 (`kill -- -$$`, `pkill -P $$`, `kill -9 -$$`) without ever being glossed.
findings.fix: Add "`$$` = the shell's own PID" to the page 1 sidebox at first use.

findings.summary: States that a trap set inside `$(...)` is lost, but it does fire when the command-substitution subshell exits — its output is silently captured into the variable.
findings.evidence: "`$(...)` also forks — a trap set there is lost" (sidebox) alongside "x=$(trap 'echo x' EXIT; :)   # dies there"
findings.fix: Reword to "`$(...)` also forks — the trap fires when the substitution ends, and its output is swallowed into the variable instead of printed".

findings.summary: The EXIT-trap page builds its examples on `$tmpdir`, `mktemp -d`, `mkfifo` and lock files, none of which are introduced until page 4.
findings.evidence: Page 3 code: "rm -rf \"${tmpdir:-}\" || true"; callout "One Dir Beats Many Files — A single `rm -rf \"$tmpdir\"` cleans everything and one trap covers all of it"; matrix rows ["mktemp -d","mkfifo"],["start child","open lock"]. Page 4 is where "`mktemp` picks randomly and atomically" and the `mktemp` modes table first appear, and `${var:-}` default expansion is never explained anywhere in the part.
findings.fix: On page 3 either use a neutral placeholder (`rm -f "$logfile"`) for the cleanup example, or add one line naming `tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)` as "a temp directory (page 4)" and gloss `${tmpdir:-}` as "empty-safe expansion"; move the "One Dir Beats Many Files" callout to page 4.

findings.summary: Claims an `exit` inside a trap can re-enter that trap, but bash marks the EXIT trap in-progress and never runs it recursively.
findings.evidence: "Careless `exit` inside a trap can re-enter it"
findings.fix: Change to: bash will not re-enter an EXIT trap that is already running, so `exit` inside cleanup is safe; disarm with `trap - EXIT INT TERM` anyway so a signal arriving mid-cleanup does not start a second handler and so cleanup is not repeated in a forked subshell.

findings.summary: Presents `mktemp -t` as a normal mode, but `-t` is deprecated in GNU coreutils and takes a prefix (not a template) on BSD/macOS.
findings.evidence: table row "`-t tpl.XXXXXX` | traceable name | same" and "tmpdir=$(mktemp -d -t iolar.XXXXXX)"
findings.fix: Use `tmpdir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/iolar.XXXXXX")` (or `mktemp -d -p "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}" iolar.XXXXXX`) as the idiom, and note in the table that `-t` is deprecated in GNU mktemp and means "prefix" on BSD/macOS.

findings.summary: A connector line is drawn straight through the "grandchild (alive)" node label in the Orphans And Grandchildren diagram, making it read as struck through.
findings.evidence: The box labelled "grandchild (alive)" has a horizontal edge line crossing the text mid-height, so it renders as "grandchild (alive)" with a strikethrough.
findings.fix: Route the child A → grandchild edge to terminate at the box border instead of passing over it, or increase the vertical gap between the child and grandchild rows so no edge crosses the label.

findings.summary: The group-kill row claims a reach the surrounding bullets say is impossible, with no explanation of why grandchildren are in the group.
findings.evidence: Bullets state "Killing a child leaves its own children alive" and "`pkill -P $$` hits direct children only, not the tree", then the table asserts ["whole group","`kill -- -$$`","entire tree"] with no supporting note that children and grandchildren inherit the process group unless they start a new one.
findings.fix: Change the reach cell to "whole process group" and add a bullet: "Grandchildren inherit the group, so a group kill reaches them — unless a child called `setsid` or started its own job control."

findings.summary: Says dash ignores an ERR trap; dash actually rejects it with a fatal `bad trap` error.
findings.evidence: "Bash pseudo-signal, not POSIX — dash ignores it"
findings.fix: Reword to "dash rejects it outright — `trap: ERR: bad trap` — and aborts the script", which makes the `#!/usr/bin/env bash` shebang point stronger.

findings.summary: The ERR/strict-mode page opens with SIGHUP and Ctrl-Z material that belongs to the interrupt chapter on page 6.
findings.evidence: Page 7 ("ERR, Strict Mode, and Stack Traces") first block: heading "Neighbours: HUP And TSTP" with "Trap HUP beside INT/TERM — SSH drops are real", "Ctrl-Z is SIGTSTP: it stops, it does not end", "Never run cleanup from a TSTP trap".
findings.fix: Move this heading and its bullets to page 6, after "Handler Hygiene", so all keyboard/terminal signals stay in the interrupt chapter; open page 7 with "When ERR Fires".
